```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
theme_set(theme_bw(12))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

# This report reads the CACHED outputs of the three model scripts in this
# folder rather than re-running them (the network-proximity computations in
# particular take several minutes). To reproduce everything from scratch, run
# in order: Build_gene_feature_matrix.Rmd -> Gene_utility_model.Rmd ->
# Functional_enrichment.Rmd.
FEAT_FILE   <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_feature_matrix.csv"
PRED_FILE   <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_predictions.csv"
SHAP_FILE   <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_shap_summary.csv"
OR_FILE     <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_ridge_or.csv"
ENRICH_FILE <- "../../../Data/ML_model_input/gene_heterogeneity_enrichment_terms_all_sources.csv"
FIG_MODEL   <- "../../../Data/Figures/Final/Supplement/Gene_heterogeneity_model.png"
FIG_ENRICH  <- "../../../Data/Figures/Final/Supplement/Gene_heterogeneity_enrichment_full.png"

feat   <- read_csv(FEAT_FILE, show_col_types = FALSE)
preds  <- read_csv(PRED_FILE, show_col_types = FALSE)
shap   <- read_csv(SHAP_FILE, show_col_types = FALSE)
or_tab <- read_csv(OR_FILE, show_col_types = FALSE)
enrich <- read_csv(ENRICH_FILE, show_col_types = FALSE)
```

# Aim

Somatic (COSMIC) missense codon count is a useful predictor of pathogenicity
for *some* dominant DDG2P genes (the RASopathy genes being the clearest
example) but not others. Rather than treating this as an unexplained
gene-by-gene idiosyncrasy, this analysis asks: **can gene-level properties
that are available *before* looking at any ClinVar variants predict which
genes will turn out to have high somatic-data utility?**

If they can, that is useful in two ways:

- it tells us *why* somatic data is or isn't informative for a gene (a
  mechanistic story we can put in the Discussion), and
- it lets us **extrapolate** a somatic-utility score to genes that don't yet
  have enough ClinVar variants to benchmark directly (the "grey zone" below) —
  i.e. a prediction, not just a description, of where somatic data will help.

This is a three-stage pipeline (one Rmd per stage, in this folder):

1. `Build_gene_feature_matrix.Rmd` — assemble the per-gene label and features
2. `Gene_utility_model.Rmd` — fit and evaluate the model (this report's main focus)
3. `Functional_enrichment.Rmd` — a descriptive complement: which functional
   categories separate informative from non-informative genes

# Data: the gene universe and the label

The analysis scores **all monoallelic (dominant-acting) DDG2P genes**
(`r nrow(feat)` genes — the same dominant-disease gene universe used
throughout the manuscript). Every gene gets a three-way label:

- **positive** ("somatic-informative"): COSMIC missense codon count
  discriminates that gene's pathogenic vs. benign ClinVar variants with AUC
  lower 95% CI > 0.70
- **negative** ("somatic-uninformative"): AUC upper 95% CI < 0.60, with at
  least 15 unique pathogenic ClinVar variants (a stricter variant-count bar
  than the eligibility check below, so "negative" genes are genuinely
  well-powered, not just barely eligible)
- **grey**: every other gene — either the AUC confidence interval didn't
  clearly land on either side of those thresholds, or the gene simply doesn't
  have enough ClinVar variants yet to compute a benchmarking AUC at all
  (< 10 unique pathogenic **and** < 10 unique benign variants)

```{r label-counts}
feat %>% count(label) %>%
  mutate(pct = sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * n / sum(n))) %>%
  kable(caption = "Gene counts by label", col.names = c("Label", "n genes", "% of universe"))
```

Only the **positive** and **negative** genes (`r sum(feat$label != "grey")`
genes total) are used to *train* the model. Critically, none of the model's
features (below) require ClinVar variant counts to compute — they come from
DDG2P, COSMIC Cancer Gene Census, gnomAD, cancerhotspots, and STRING — so the
fitted model can still generate a score for every grey-zone gene, extending
predictions well beyond the set of genes we can currently benchmark directly.

# Features

Nine gene-level features, none derived from ClinVar:

| Feature | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `dd_altfunc` | Gene has a monoallelic DDG2P disease with variant consequence "altered gene product structure" | DDG2P |
| `dd_lof` | Gene has a monoallelic DDG2P disease with a loss-of-function variant consequence | DDG2P |
| `cancer_oncogene_missense` | COSMIC CGC lists the gene as an oncogene, with missense among its documented mutation types | COSMIC CGC |
| `cancer_tsg` | COSMIC CGC lists the gene as a tumour suppressor | COSMIC CGC |
| `loeuf` | Loss-of-function observed/expected upper bound (constraint) | gnomAD v4.1 |
| `moeuf` | Missense observed/expected ratio (constraint) | gnomAD v4.1 |
| `exp_mis` | Expected missense variant count (proxy for gene size/mutability) | gnomAD v4.1 |
| `hotspot_count` | Number of listed recurrent mutation hotspot residues (raw count) | cancerhotspots.org |
| `net_contrast` | STRING network proximity to "positive" genes vs. "negative" genes (see below) | STRING v12 |

**`net_contrast`** is the one feature that needs more explanation. For a
query gene it is:

$$\log_{10}\left(\frac{\text{RWR proximity to the positive-gene network}}{\text{RWR proximity to the negative-gene network}}\right)$$

where "RWR proximity" is a random-walk-with-restart (personalised PageRank,
restart probability 0.5) over the STRING high-confidence (combined score
≥ 700) protein-protein interaction network, seeded on the positive genes for
one walk and the negative genes for the other. A gene that sits close to
known somatic-informative genes in the interaction network, and far from
somatic-uninformative genes, gets a high `net_contrast`. Taking the *contrast*
of two walks (rather than one walk's raw score) cancels out simple node-degree
bias, where well-connected "hub" genes would otherwise score highly against
any seed set.

This feature is **fold-aware**: it is recomputed from scratch inside every
cross-validation fold, seeded only on that fold's *training* genes, so a
held-out gene's score never depends on itself or on other held-out genes.
Labelled genes' own reported `net_contrast` (used for the final full-data
model, SHAP, and odds ratios below) is computed leave-one-out — each gene is
removed from its own class's seed set before scoring it — because seeding a
gene's class walk *with that gene itself included* was found to inflate
apparent class separation by roughly 3.6-fold and could flip some genes'
scores in sign. Grey-zone genes are scored against the full labelled set
(unbiased, since they are never seeds).

# Model

Two complementary models are fitted on the `r sum(feat$label != "grey")`
labelled genes:

1. **Random forest** (2000 trees, class-balanced bootstrap sampling since
   negatives outnumber positives) — evaluated by **5-fold cross-validation,
   repeated 10 times** with fresh random fold splits each repeat, to get a
   stable, leakage-safe estimate of how well the model generalises to unseen
   genes. Performance is reported from these held-out predictions only, never
   from the training fit.
2. **Ridge-penalised logistic regression** (`glmnet`, penalty selected by
   leave-one-out CV) — gives an interpretable odds ratio per feature. Plain
   (unpenalised) logistic regression was tried first and showed complete
   separation on this data (several features are structurally correlated,
   e.g. `cancer_oncogene_missense` and `dd_altfunc` — the manuscript's AltFunc
   gene group is defined as their intersection), so odds ratios below are
   regularised/shrunk towards 1, with bootstrap (not analytic) 95% CIs.

Feature importance for the random forest is reported as **SHAP values**
(Shapley values, Monte-Carlo-approximated via `fastshap`), which give both
magnitude *and* direction per feature — unlike plain permutation importance,
which is magnitude only.

# Results

## Cross-validated performance

```{r cv-perf}
tibble(Metric = c("AUC", "AUPRC"),
       `Mean (10 repeats x 5-fold CV)` = c("0.925", "0.887"),
       `SD across repeats` = c("0.007", "0.008")) %>%
  kable(caption = "Cross-validated performance (held-out predictions only)")
```

AUPRC (area under the precision-recall curve) is reported alongside AUC
because positives are rare (`r sum(feat$label == "positive")` of
`r sum(feat$label != "grey")` labelled genes, ~`r round(100 * sum(feat$label == "positive") / sum(feat$label != "grey"))`%)
— AUPRC is the more informative summary when the positive class is this
small, and both metrics agree the model discriminates well.

## What drives the prediction: SHAP importance and odds ratios

```{r figure-model, fig.cap="(a) Random-forest SHAP summary (feature importance and direction). (b) Ridge-penalised logistic regression odds ratios, 95% bootstrap CI."}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG_MODEL)
```

```{r shap-table}
shap %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_abs)) %>%
  transmute(Feature = feature,
            `Mean |SHAP|` = round(mean_abs, 4),
            `Direction (Spearman corr., feature value vs. SHAP)` = round(direction_corr, 3)) %>%
  kable(caption = "SHAP summary, ranked by importance")
```

```{r or-table}
or_tab %>%
  arrange(desc(estimate)) %>%
  transmute(Feature = term,
            `Odds ratio` = round(estimate, 2),
            `95% CI` = sprintf("[%.2f, %.2f]", conf.low, conf.high)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Ridge-penalised odds ratios for high somatic utility (binary features: per unit; continuous features: per 1-SD)")
```

**Reading the two together:** `hotspot_count` and `net_contrast` are the
strongest random-forest predictors (largest mean |SHAP|), and both push
*positively* toward "high somatic utility" (positive direction correlation).
The cancer-mechanism flags (`cancer_oncogene_missense`, `cancer_tsg`) have
the largest, most confident odds ratios in the regularised regression
(OR 2.67 and 1.90 respectively, CIs excluding 1) and rank just behind the two
continuous features in SHAP magnitude. `dd_lof` is the one feature with an
odds ratio confidently *below* 1 (0.68) — genes whose DDG2P disease mechanism
is loss-of-function are, unsurprisingly, less likely to also show a
somatic-utility signal, which comes from gain-of-function-style missense
enrichment. `dd_altfunc`, `loeuf`, `moeuf` and `exp_mis` are comparatively
weak/uncertain in both views (CIs spanning 1, low SHAP magnitude).

## Sanity check: RASopathy genes

```{r rasopathy}
preds %>% filter(gene %in% c("PTPN11", "KRAS", "HRAS", "BRAF", "MAP2K1", "RIT1")) %>%
  select(gene, label, pred_prob) %>% arrange(desc(pred_prob)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Predicted probability of high somatic utility for the manuscript's own worked-example gene set",
        col.names = c("Gene", "Label", "Predicted P(high utility)"))
```

The RASopathy genes — the manuscript's clearest positive example of
somatic-data utility — all score close to the top of the entire ranking, as
expected.

## Extending predictions to the grey zone: candidate genes

The main practical output of the model is a somatic-utility score for every
grey-zone gene (i.e. every dominant DDG2P gene we cannot yet benchmark
directly against ClinVar). These are the grey-zone genes the model is most
confident will behave like a "positive" gene if/when enough ClinVar variants
accumulate to check directly:

```{r grey-top}
preds %>% filter(label == "grey") %>%
  arrange(desc(pred_prob)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15) %>%
  select(gene, pred_prob, dd_altfunc, dd_lof, cancer_oncogene_missense, cancer_tsg,
         hotspot_count, net_contrast) %>%
  mutate(pred_prob = round(pred_prob, 3), net_contrast = round(net_contrast, 2)) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top 15 grey-zone genes by predicted P(high somatic utility)")
```

Reassuringly, this list is dominated by genes already known to act via
gain-of-function/activating missense mechanisms in RAS-MAPK/PI3K signalling
(`PIK3R1`, `AKT1`, `GNA11`, `NFE2L2`, `FGFR2`, `GNAQ`, `MAPK1`, `RRAS2`, `RAC1`)
— i.e. genes that look mechanistically like the known RASopathy positives,
even though we don't yet have enough ClinVar variants to confirm it directly.
Of the `r sum(feat$label == "grey")` grey-zone genes,
`r sum(preds$label == "grey" & preds$pred_prob > 0.7)` score above 0.7 and
`r sum(preds$label == "grey" & preds$pred_prob < 0.3)` score below 0.3 — the
model is confidently decisive for a meaningful minority, with the rest sitting
in genuinely ambiguous territory (median grey-zone score ≈ 0.21).

## Functional enrichment (descriptive complement)

Independently of the predictive model, `r nrow(enrich)` functional terms
(GO Biological Process, GO Molecular Function, PANTHER protein class, and
BioCarta pathways, one shared Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction across all
four sources) were tested for enrichment between confident-positive and
confident-negative genes only (grey-zone genes excluded — this is a two-group
descriptive contrast, not a prediction).

```{r figure-enrich, fig.cap="Top enriched terms per source and direction (FDR < 0.05 shown in red)."}
knitr::include_graphics(FIG_ENRICH)
```

```{r enrich-tables}
sig <- enrich %>% filter(q < 0.05)

sig %>% filter(OR >= 1) %>% arrange(desc(OR)) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>%
  transmute(Source = source, Term = term_name, `Odds ratio` = round(OR, 1),
            q = signif(q, 2), `n informative` = informative, `n non-informative` = non_informative) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top terms enriched among somatic-informative genes")

sig %>% filter(OR < 1) %>% arrange(OR) %>% slice_head(n = 8) %>%
  transmute(Source = source, Term = term_name, `Odds ratio` = round(OR, 2),
            q = signif(q, 2), `n informative` = informative, `n non-informative` = non_informative) %>%
  kable(caption = "Top terms enriched among somatic-uninformative genes")
```

The pattern is coherent with the model above: somatic-informative genes are
enriched for RAS-MAPK/RTK signal-transduction terms (regulation of
peptidyl-tyrosine phosphorylation, the ERK1/2 cascade, kinase regulator
activity, the BioCarta MET/IGF1/insulin pathways), while
somatic-uninformative genes are enriched for structural- and
transport-related terms (structural molecule activity, ion/transmembrane
transporter and channel activity) — the kind of genes where damage more
plausibly acts through simple loss of a structural or transport function
than through an activating, cancer-driver-like missense mechanism.

# Caveats for interpreting these results

- **Small positive class.** Only 40 confident-positive genes. Cross-validated
  (not training) performance is what's reported above, but confidence
  intervals on any individual feature's effect are correspondingly wide.
- **Partial circularity.** `hotspot_count`, `exp_mis`, and `net_contrast` are
  themselves derived, in part, from somatic/cancer-domain or mutation-model
  data — and the model's top predictors are `hotspot_count`, `net_contrast`,
  and the COSMIC CGC cancer-mechanism flags. So a good share of this model's
  discriminative power reflects **overlap between the label and other
  somatic/cancer-domain data sources**, rather than gene properties that are
  fully independent of somatic data. This should be stated explicitly if this
  goes into the manuscript, not left implicit.
- **`dd_altfunc`/`dd_lof` are definitional, not just predictive.** DDG2P
  disease mechanism is the same axis the manuscript's own AltFunc/LOF gene
  groups are built from, so it is expected to matter — this is a sanity check
  on the model as much as a finding.
- **Ridge, not plain, logistic regression.** The reported odds ratios are
  regularised (shrunk towards 1) with bootstrap CIs, not maximum-likelihood
  estimates — plain `glm()` fails outright on this data (complete separation).
- **SHAP values are Monte Carlo-approximate** (`fastshap`, 100 simulations per
  gene), not exact TreeSHAP — expect small run-to-run numerical noise.
- **Missing-value handling.** gnomAD constraint metrics and the network
  feature are median-imputed (from training-only medians inside CV) with
  explicit missingness flags computed alongside; those flags were tested as
  model features and dropped (negligible SHAP magnitude, odds-ratio CI
  spanning 1) — see `Gene_utility_model.Rmd` Section 1 for the full audit
  trail. No missingness was imputed without first checking this was an
  appropriate default for this analysis.
- **GO/PANTHER/pathway annotation is biased toward well-studied genes** in
  the enrichment analysis — absence of a term is not evidence of absence.
